title: State ex rel. Office of the State Engineer v. Intrepid Potash, Inc.
description: Whether Intrepid Potash, Inc. abandoned its water rights in the Pecos River, with the plaintiff (Office of the State Engineer) arguing that Intrepid abandoned most of its water rights due to nonuse and speculation, and the defendant (Intrepid Potash, Inc.) arguing that it did not intend to abandon its rights and took steps to preserve them.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that Intrepid abandoned all but 150 acre-feet per year (afy) of its Pecos River water rights due to prolonged nonuse and speculation, which is inconsistent with the constitutional mandate of beneficial use.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that it did not intend to abandon its water rights, citing efforts to sell, lease, or transfer the rights, file extensions of time, and improve diversion structures, and that economic/legal obstacles excused nonuse.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, concluding that Intrepid abandoned all but 150 afy of its Pecos River water rights and that water speculation is contrary to beneficial use.

title: State v. Perea
description: Whether information provided by a confidential informant (CI) in a search warrant application satisfies the probable cause requirement under Article II, Section 10 of the New Mexico Constitution, with the plaintiff arguing it does and the defendant arguing it does not.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the affidavit established the CI had personal knowledge from first-hand observations of methamphetamine in the Petitioner's home, consistent with trafficking, which constitutes an adequate basis of knowledge for probable cause.
defendant_argument: The Petitioner argued the affidavit failed to demonstrate the CI's basis of knowledge with sufficient detail regarding the amount, packaging, or observed sales of methamphetamine, and that the warrant was overbroad.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' reversal of the district court's grant of the motion to suppress, thereby upholding the search warrant.

title: Bolen v. New Mexico Racing Commission
description: Whether judicial immunity is a defense available to a public body sued under the New Mexico Civil Rights Act (CRA).
plaintiff_argument: Bolen argued that judicial immunity protects individuals, not governmental entities, and therefore a public body may not rely on it in defense of a CRA claim.
defendant_argument: NMRC argued that the CRA's plain language establishes that judicial immunity is an available defense for a public body.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed that judicial immunity is an available defense for public bodies under the CRA but reversed the Court of Appeals' decision that NMRC was immune, remanding the case to the district court for further proceedings to apply a new framework for determining immunity.

title: Stewart v. Ramczyk
description: Whether Senate President Pro Tempore Mimi Stewart is entitled to legislative immunity under the New Mexico Constitution's Speech or Debate Clause for reassigning Senator Jacob Candelaria's office and Senate floor seat, and whether a court can examine her motives to determine this immunity.
plaintiff_argument: Stewart argued that her actions of reassigning Candelaria's office and seat were legitimate legislative activities, making her entitled to legislative immunity and her motives irrelevant.
defendant_argument: Candelaria argued that Stewart's actions were unlawful retaliation, not legitimate legislative activities, and that the court should examine her motives, interpreting the New Mexico Speech or Debate Clause more narrowly.
decision_outcome: The court granted the writ of superintending control, holding that Stewart's motive is irrelevant and that she is entitled to legislative immunity, remanding the case to dismiss Candelaria's complaint.

title: State v. Maestas
description: Whether a contempt fine ordered payable to a third party is permitted under statute and the New Mexico Constitution, with the plaintiff arguing it is permitted and constitutional, and the defendant arguing it is not permitted and must be paid directly to the court.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that the constitutional provision on fees does not prohibit courts from imposing fines payable to other entities, nor does it require such fines to be collected by the court, as fines are not fees.
defendant_argument: Maestas argues that contempt fines must be paid directly to the court and that allowing judges to direct fines to third parties could be an unlawful way for judges to retain a benefit similar to compensation.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the contempt fine payable to a third party was permitted under the judiciary's inherent contempt power and is constitutional, affirming the district court's order.

title: Amdor v. Grisham
description: Whether the Governor's emergency orders declaring gun violence and drug abuse as public health emergencies exceed the scope of the Public Health Emergency Response Act (PHERA), the proper scope of the police power, and violate separation-of-powers principles.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argued that the emergency orders exceeded the Governor's authority under PHERA, were an improper exercise of police power, and violated separation-of-powers principles because gun violence and drug abuse are not true public health emergencies under PHERA, and the orders encroached on legislative functions.
defendant_argument: The respondents argued that the emergency orders were within the Governor's authority under PHERA, were a proper exercise of police power, and did not violate separation-of-powers principles, as PHERA provides broad authority to respond to public health emergencies, and the orders were temporary measures.
decision_outcome: The court denied most of the petition, ruling that the emergency orders regarding gun violence and drug abuse did not violate the PHERA or separation-of-powers doctrine, but granted the petition to strike down the suspension of the Juvenile Detention Alternatives Initiative (JDAI) program as exceeding police power.

title: Johnson v. Board of Education
description: Whether public schools are considered public accommodations under the New Mexico Human Rights Act, making them subject to anti-discrimination laws.
plaintiff_argument: Public schools are public accommodations under the NMHRA, and thus discriminatory conduct within them is unlawful.
defendant_argument: Public schools are not public accommodations under the NMHRA, and therefore not subject to its anti-discrimination provisions.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, holding that public schools are public accommodations under the NMHRA and overruling prior inconsistent precedent.

title: State v. Vasquez
description: Whether a district court has the authority to independently initiate suppression hearings for warrantless searches, or if it must wait for a party to raise the issue.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the district court lacked standing and jurisdiction to sua sponte raise suppression issues, violated the separation of powers, and demonstrated bias by doing so.
defendant_argument: The defendant implicitly supported the district court's inherent authority to raise suppression issues sua sponte to protect fundamental rights against unreasonable searches and seizures.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the district court's inherent authority and jurisdiction to sua sponte raise suppression issues for warrantless searches, finding that such actions do not violate separation of powers or inherently demonstrate bias.

title: Johnson & Johnson v. Wilson
description: Whether the New Mexico Office of the Attorney General (OAG), when representing the State in civil litigation, has the discovery authority to obtain and produce documents and information from a state executive agency that is not a named party to the litigation.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners (Johnson & Johnson) argued that the State's discovery obligations extend to its constituent agencies, and therefore, the Attorney General has the authority and obligation to produce documents from non-party executive agencies.
defendant_argument: The State (through the Attorney General) argued that the OAG lacks possession, custody, or control of documents held by other gubernatorially controlled state agencies, and that compelling such production would infringe on separation of powers principles.
decision_outcome: The court granted the petition for writ of superintending control, vacated the district court's discovery order, and remanded the matter with instructions to compel the production of relevant documents and information from the executive agencies.

title: State ex. rel. Raúl Torrez v. Board of County Commissioners for Lea County
description: Whether county and municipal officials exceeded their authority by enacting local ordinances regulating abortion and abortion providers, which the State argues are preempted by state law.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that the local ordinances regulating abortion are preempted by state law, including the Health Care Freedom Act, and violate the New Mexico Constitution's Equal Rights Amendment.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that the ordinances are a lawful exercise of their police powers, merely enforce federal law (Comstock Act), and do not restrict abortion access as no providers operate in their jurisdictions, thus preemption is not applicable.
decision_outcome: The court granted the writ of mandamus, ruling that the local ordinances regulating abortion are preempted by state law and prohibiting their enforcement.

title: Aztec Municipal Schools v. Cardenas
description: Whether the Workers' Compensation Act's limits on disability benefits for secondary mental impairments, which are not imposed on secondary physical impairments, violate the Equal Protection Clause of the New Mexico Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that the Workers' Compensation Act discriminates against workers with secondary mental impairments by limiting their disability benefits to 150 weeks, while workers with secondary physical impairments could receive up to 500 weeks, thereby violating the Equal Protection Clause.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that workers with secondary mental impairments are not similarly situated to those with secondary physical impairments, and that there is a logical relationship between the duration and severity of a secondary mental impairment and the nature of the physical injury that caused it.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that Sections 52-1-41(C) and -42(A)(4) of the Workers' Compensation Act, which treat workers with secondary mental impairments differently than similarly situated workers with secondary physical impairments, violate the Equal Protection Clause of the New Mexico Constitution. The case was remanded for further proceedings.

title: State ex rel. Candelaria v. Grisham
description: Whether the legislative or executive branch controls the allocation and expenditure of federal American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funds received by the state.
plaintiff_argument: The Legislature has the authority to appropriate the ARPA funds because they are public money and Congress did not designate them for specific state programs or agencies, making them subject to legislative appropriation under the state constitution.
defendant_argument: The Governor has the authority to administer the federal funds, arguing that the Legislature lacks the power to appropriate federal funds, especially since they are held in a suspense account and are not yet considered the absolute property of the state.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the ARPA funds are subject to legislative appropriation and issued a prohibitory writ of mandamus preventing the Governor and State Treasurer from expending additional ARPA funds without legislative appropriation.

title: State v. Ayon
description: Whether a district court judge has the authority at a preliminary hearing to decide if evidence was obtained from an unconstitutional search or seizure, with the State arguing against such authority and the defendant arguing for it.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the district court exceeded its authority by ruling on the legality of evidence at a preliminary hearing, asserting that preliminary hearings and grand jury proceedings share a common purpose and should have congruent rules regarding evidence exclusion.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the district court has the authority to exclude illegally obtained evidence at a preliminary hearing, citing substantial differences between grand jury proceedings and preliminary hearings, and the New Mexico Constitution's protection against unconstitutional searches and seizures.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' reversal, holding that a district court judge lacks the authority at a preliminary examination to decide whether evidence was obtained from an unconstitutional search or seizure.

title: Grisham v. Van Soelen
description: Whether a partisan gerrymandering claim is cognizable and justiciable under the Equal Protection Clause of Article II, Section 18 of the New Mexico Constitution, and if so, what standards should be applied in its adjudication.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff (Real Parties in Interest) argued that the 2021 congressional districting maps constitute an unconstitutional partisan gerrymander under New Mexico's Equal Protection Clause, leading to vote dilution and entrenchment of one political party.
defendant_argument: The defendant (Petitioners) argued that partisan gerrymandering claims are nonjusticiable political questions, that the New Mexico Equal Protection Clause is coextensive with the federal one which does not prohibit partisan gerrymandering, and that judicial review would violate separation of powers.
decision_outcome: The New Mexico Supreme Court ruled that partisan gerrymandering claims are justiciable under Article II, Section 18 of the New Mexico Constitution, adopting Justice Kagan's three-part test and applying intermediate scrutiny.

title: Indigenous Lifeways v. New Mexico Compilation Commission Advisory Committee
description: Whether Constitutional Amendment 1 is void because it violates the constitutional prohibition against logrolling by combining multiple independent measures into a single ballot question, or because its ballot title was misleading, with petitioners arguing it is void and respondents arguing it is constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argued that Amendment 1 logrolled multiple independent measures into a single-ballot question, violating the single-measure rule, and that its ballot title was misleading, thus rendering its ratification null and void.
defendant_argument: The Advisory Committee and Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham argued that the petition was untimely, and on the merits, that Amendment 1 did not violate the constitutional prohibition against logrolling and its ballot title was not misleading.
decision_outcome: The court denied the petition for writ of mandamus, ruling that Constitutional Amendment 1 did not violate the single-measure rule or the constitutional prohibition against logrolling, and that its ballot title was not misleading.

title: State v. Granados
description: Whether the NEU agents had reasonable suspicion to stop Defendant and whether Defendant's seizure was unreasonable under Article II, Section 10 of the New Mexico Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the agents possessed reasonable suspicion to stop Defendant and that Defendant was not seized at the gas station because he fled.
defendant_argument: Defendant argued that the NEU agents lacked a legitimate basis to stop him, that the confidential informant's tip was unreliable, and that his seizure was unreasonable under the New Mexico Constitution.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals, holding that Defendant's seizure was unreasonable under Article II, Section 10 of the New Mexico Constitution, and remanded the case with instructions to grant the motion to suppress.

title: State ex rel. Office of the State Engineer v. Romero
description: Whether an owner of a groundwater right may forfeit part or all of a claimed water right, or if any use, no matter how small, preserves the right to the whole.
plaintiff_argument: The Office of the State Engineer argued that New Mexico's groundwater forfeiture statute allows for partial forfeiture, meaning that nonuse of a portion of a water right can lead to its forfeiture.
defendant_argument: Toby Romero argued that his limited use of water should preserve his entire claimed water right, asserting that any use, no matter how small, negates forfeiture of the larger right, and that forfeiture should only apply to deliberate waste or unauthorized use, not nonuse.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's decision, ruling that the groundwater forfeiture statute allows for partial forfeiture, consistent with the constitutional doctrine of beneficial use, and that substantial evidence supported the finding of nonuse by the petitioner.

title: Adobe Whitewater Club of New Mexico v. New Mexico State Game Commission
description: Whether the public's right to recreate and fish in public water, which flows over private property, also allows the public the right to touch the privately owned beds below those waters, with petitioners arguing for this right and intervenors arguing against it based on private property trespass.
plaintiff_argument: The Regulations are unconstitutional because Article XVI, Section 2 and the court's prior decision in Red River implicitly recognize the public's right to use streambeds and banks as reasonably necessary for the enjoyment of public waters.
defendant_argument: The Regulations do not privatize or close public waters but rather express the existing right of landowners to exclude trespassers from privately owned riverbeds, asserting that walking or wading on privately owned beds constitutes trespass.
decision_outcome: The court concluded that the Regulations are an unconstitutional infringement on the public's right to use public water and that the Commission lacked the legislative authority to promulgate them, holding that the public has the right to recreate and fish in public waters, including acts reasonably necessary for enjoyment, such as touching streambeds.

title: Anderson v. State
description: Whether inmates and nonprofit organizations must exhaust administrative remedies with the New Mexico Corrections Department (NMCD) before seeking judicial relief for alleged constitutional violations related to COVID-19 management in prisons.
plaintiff_argument: Plaintiffs argued that the exhaustion requirement is an unconstitutional limitation on habeas corpus jurisdiction, that it would be futile because NMCD cannot grant the requested relief (release), and that vicarious exhaustion should satisfy the requirement for the entire class.
defendant_argument: Defendants argued that the district court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction because the Named Plaintiffs failed to exhaust administrative remedies as required by statute and rule, and that the futility exception does not apply.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the district court's dismissal of the amended complaint, holding that plaintiffs failed to exhaust administrative remedies and did not demonstrate futility.

title: State v. Mascareno-Haidle
description: Whether the State must prove by clear and convincing evidence that no release conditions will reasonably protect the safety of any other person or the community to justify pretrial detention, or if the nature and circumstances of the charged offense alone are sufficient.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the nature and circumstances of the defendant's alleged dangerous conduct should be sufficient, by itself, to sustain the burden of proving that no release conditions would reasonably protect community safety, thereby requesting a less stringent evidentiary standard.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the State failed to meet its evidentiary burden to prove that no release conditions could reasonably protect the safety of the community, and that the defendant had complied with previously imposed release conditions.
decision_outcome: The court upheld the Court of Appeals' affirmance of the district court's denial of pretrial detention, ruling that the State failed to meet its evidentiary burden to prove that no release conditions would reasonably protect the safety of the community.

title: State v. Hildreth
description: Whether judicial conduct at trial may result in a bar to retrial under the double jeopardy clause of the New Mexico Constitution, and if so, whether the district court judge's conduct in this case bars retrial.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the Breit test, which concerns prosecutorial misconduct, should not apply to judicial conduct, and even if it did, the judge's actions did not meet the criteria to bar retrial.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the district court judge's conduct during trial denied his right to effective assistance of counsel and should bar retrial on double jeopardy grounds under the Breit test.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' reversal of the defendant's conviction and ruled that the district court judge's conduct satisfied the Breit test, thereby barring retrial under the double jeopardy clause.

title: State v. Wright
description: Whether the arrest of Defendant Somer D. Wright by a noncommissioned, volunteer reserve deputy, in violation of statutory requirements, was constitutionally unreasonable under Article II, Section 10 of the New Mexico Constitution, thereby warranting suppression of evidence.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the detention, even if unlawful, was constitutionally reasonable as it was in furtherance of an important interest (deterring drunk driving) and the privacy intrusion was minimal, thus not warranting suppression.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the arrest by a noncommissioned deputy was illegal and constitutionally unreasonable under Article II, Section 10 of the New Mexico Constitution, violating her privacy interests and requiring suppression of all evidence obtained.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, ruling that the arrest was illegal and violated the New Mexico Constitution, and required suppression of all evidence obtained as a result of the arrest.

title: Citizens for Fair Rates & the Environment v. New Mexico Public Regulation Commission
description: Whether the Energy Transition Act (ETA) is constitutional and whether the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission's final order approving a financing order for the abandonment of San Juan Generating Station Units 1 and 4 complies with statutory requirements.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, New Energy, argued that the ETA is unconstitutional on various grounds, including due process, separation of powers, affecting pending cases, impairing contractual/vested rights, log-rolling, amending statutes by reference, and special legislation, and that the Commission's final order regarding the securities firm memorandum was in error.
defendant_argument: The defendant, New Mexico Public Regulation Commission, and intervenors like Public Service Company of New Mexico, defended the constitutionality of the ETA and asserted that the Commission's final order was based on a reasonable construction of the statute and supported by substantial evidence.
decision_outcome: The court rejected New Energy's constitutional challenges to the ETA and affirmed the final order of the Commission granting PNM's application for a financing order in connection with its abandonment of San Juan Units One and Four.

title: State v. Wilson
description: Whether the State's public health orders (PHOs) during the COVID-19 pandemic constitute a compensable taking of private property under the New Mexico Constitution or the Public Health Emergency Response Act.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that PHOs are a valid exercise of police power to protect public health and do not constitute a compensable taking, and that statutory compensation is limited to health care-related property.
defendant_argument: The businesses argued that the PHOs' restrictions on private property are "unprecedented" and require just compensation, and that the statutory compensation provision should be interpreted broadly.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the public health orders (PHOs) cannot support a claim for a regulatory taking requiring compensation under either the New Mexico Constitution or the Public Health Emergency Response Act, and claimants under the Act must exhaust administrative remedies.

title: Siebert v.  Okun
description: Whether the cap on nonmedical and nonpunitive damages under the Medical Malpractice Act (MMA) violates the right to trial by jury guaranteed by Article II, Section 12 of the New Mexico Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the MMA damages cap is unconstitutional, specifically violating the right to a jury trial by limiting the jury's exclusive province to determine the full amount of damages.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the MMA damages cap is constitutional, does not violate the right to a jury trial, and merely gives legal effect to the jury's damages award without invading the jury's role as fact-finder.
decision_outcome: The court held that the MMA nonmedical, nonpunitive damages cap does not violate the constitutional right to trial by jury and reversed the district court's denial of the defendants' motion to conform the judgment to the statutory cap.

title: City of Albuquerque v. SMP Properties, LLC
description: Whether precondemnation activity by the City of Albuquerque that allegedly caused a tenant to terminate its lease constitutes substantial interference with property use, giving rise to an inverse condemnation claim for compensable consequential damages.
plaintiff_argument: The City of Albuquerque argued that its precondemnation activities did not substantially interfere with SMP's property use and that the lost lease value was not a compensable element of damages.
defendant_argument: SMP Properties, LLC argued that Albuquerque's precondemnation communications directly caused its tenant, SAIA, to terminate its lease, constituting substantial interference and resulting in compensable lost rental income and property devaluation.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals' reversal of the district court's grant of partial summary judgment, remanding the case for further proceedings to determine if substantial interference occurred and to assess damages.

title: Grisham v. Romero
description: Whether the executive branch is authorized to restrict or close businesses for public health protection, and whether the temporary closure of indoor dining mandated by the July 13, 2020, emergency public health order was arbitrary and capricious.
plaintiff_argument: The July Order's indoor dining ban was ultra vires, unenforceable, unreasonable, arbitrary, and capricious, exceeding legislative powers and usurping procedural requirements for quarantine orders.
defendant_argument: The executive branch is authorized to restrict businesses for public health, and the July Order's temporary closure of indoor dining was a reasonable and necessary policy choice, not arbitrary or capricious.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the executive branch was authorized to issue the public health order restricting businesses, and the temporary closure of indoor dining was neither arbitrary nor capricious, vacating the district court's temporary restraining order.
